title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Brute force to optimized: O(n squared) DP scanning every earlier index versus an O(n log n) tails array with binary search.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements need not be contiguous, but must appear in the same relative order and be strictly increasing).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums array"],["Output","Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence"],["Key Insight","Maintaining the smallest possible \"tail\" value for every achievable subsequence length allows binary search to place each new number in O(log n)"],["Constraints","Up to 2500 numbers"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Longest increasing subsequence\"","A well-known DP problem with an O(n squared) direct solution, and a faster O(n log n) solution using a cleverly maintained \"tails\" array plus binary search"]]}

blocks.text: A direct DP defines dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence ENDING exactly at index i, built from every earlier index j where nums[j] is smaller. A faster approach instead maintains an array "tails", where tails[k] is the SMALLEST possible value that could end an increasing subsequence of length k+1 seen so far; processing numbers left to right and binary searching for each number's correct position in tails maintains this invariant in O(log n) per number.

blocks.title: Analogy: Keeping the Most "Promising" Ending Value for Each Possible Streak Length
blocks.text: Picture tracking, for every possible streak length achieved so far, the SMALLEST possible ending value for a streak of that length, since a smaller ending value leaves more room for future numbers to extend it. Each new number either extends the longest streak so far, or improves (lowers) the ending value of some shorter streak, found via a quick bisecting search.

blocks.caption: The tails array tracks the smallest ending value for each achievable subsequence length, updated via binary search

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A direct O(n squared) DP defines dp[i] as the LIS ending at index i, built from every earlier smaller-valued index, but this revisits many index pairs.

Observation 2: Maintaining an array "tails", where tails[k] holds the SMALLEST possible ending value achievable for an increasing subsequence of length k+1, captures everything needed without tracking every individual subsequence explicitly.

Observation 3: For each new number, binary searching tails for the first position where the number could replace an existing (larger) tail value, or extend the array if it is larger than every current tail, correctly maintains this invariant.

Observation 4: The FINAL LENGTH of the tails array (not its contents, which do not represent an actual valid subsequence) is exactly the length of the longest increasing subsequence.
This leads to maintaining a tails array and binary searching for each number's insertion point, achieving O(n log n) overall.
Use direct O(n squared) DP: dp[i] is the LIS length ending at index i, built by scanning every earlier index j and checking if nums[j] is smaller.
Why the code is written this way

items: Scanning every earlier index directly implements the "ending at i" DP definition clearly.
This costs O(n squared), correct but slower than needed; maintaining a tails array with binary search achieves O(n log n) instead.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared).
Space: O(n) for the dp array.
Limitation: maintaining a tails array with binary search per number brings this down to O(n log n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain an initially empty array tails. For each number in nums, binary search tails for the leftmost position where the current number could be inserted to keep tails sorted (a lower-bound search). If that position is at the end of tails, append the number (it extends the longest subsequence found so far). Otherwise, overwrite tails at that position with the current number (it improves, meaning lowers, the ending value for a subsequence of that length, without changing the achieved length itself). After processing all numbers, the LENGTH of tails is the answer.
Maintain a tails array, binary searching for each number's correct position to either extend or improve it.

blocks.text: The tails array always stays sorted and represents, at every point, the smallest achievable ending value for every subsequence length seen so far; replacing a larger tail with a smaller equal-length ending value never reduces the achievable length, and can only help future numbers extend further, so the final length of tails correctly equals the true longest increasing subsequence length, even though the CONTENTS of tails do not represent one single actual valid subsequence.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), a binary search per number.
Space: O(n) for the tails array.

blocks.text: Longest Increasing Subsequence is a landmark DP problem with a well-known faster alternative: maintaining the smallest achievable tail per length, using binary search.

items: Believing the final tails array itself represents an actual longest increasing subsequence (it does not, only its LENGTH is meaningful).
Using an upper-bound search instead of a lower-bound (leftmost) search, which would incorrectly handle duplicate values for the STRICTLY increasing requirement.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["All numbers strictly increasing already","The answer is the full array length."],["All numbers identical","The answer is 1 (a single element, since strictly increasing forbids repeats)."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "the tails array is a bookkeeping trick, not an actual subsequence" prevents a very common misunderstanding of this technique when explaining it.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "longest increasing subsequence, can you do better than O(n squared)", think: a tails array maintained via binary search, O(n log n).

items: How would you reconstruct one actual longest increasing subsequence, not just its length, using this same technique?
Russian Doll Envelopes and Longest Chain of Pairs, both build on this same tails-array binary search technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The O(n squared) DP approach is correct and simpler; the tails-array approach costs O(n log n), the optimal solution for this problem.

items: Pattern: maintaining the smallest achievable "tail" value per subsequence length, updated via binary search.
Core Idea: each number either extends the tails array (a new longest length) or replaces a tail to improve future extensibility.
Time: O(n squared) for the direct DP, O(n log n) for the tails-array approach.
Most Important Observation: the tails array's length, not its contents, is the meaningful answer.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, frequently asked medium-level DP problem with a well-known faster twist.
One line memory trick: smallest tail per length, found by binary search.
